message.content:
The sea typically looks blue—especially when it’s clear and calm—because water absorbs longer wavelengths (red, orange, yellow) more strongly than shorter wavelengths (blue). When sunlight hits the surface, the shorter blue wavelengths scatter in all directions, giving the ocean its characteristic hue.

However, the exact shade can change depending on several factors:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Depth** | Deeper water tends to appear darker blue or even greenish‑black because more light is absorbed. |
| **Algae & phytoplankton** | High concentrations give the water a greenish tint. |
| **Sediment & turbidity** | Suspended particles can make the water look brownish or murky. |
| **Sun angle & weather** | Low sun angles (sunrise/sunset) can produce pink or orange hues; overcast skies often make the sea look grayish. |
| **Water composition** | Presence of dissolved minerals or organic matter can shift the color toward turquoise or teal. |

So while “blue” is the most common description, the sea’s color is actually a dynamic blend influenced by depth, biological activity, sediment, and lighting conditions.
